name: Kabul
info: Kabul is a city high in a narrow valley of the Hindu Kush in eastern Afghanistan, believed to be over 3,500 years old, held by many empires and the capital of Afghanistan since 1776.

facts.founded: The origin of Kabul, who built it and when, is largely unknown; the city is believed to be over 3,500 years old, and the Rigveda and the Avesta refer to a settlement called Kubha.
facts.where: At an altitude of 1,791 metres in a narrow valley of the Hindu Kush, on the Kabul River, in the eastern half of Afghanistan.
facts.known: A city of the Achaemenid, Mauryan, Kushan and Mughal worlds; Babur's headquarters and burial place; the capital of the Durrani Empire from 1776; the Anglo-Afghan wars; the gardens and palaces of Bagh-e Babur and Darul Aman; the wars from 1978 to 2001
facts.today: Kabul is the capital and largest city of Afghanistan.

t: Kabul lay on trade routes between India, Persia and Central Asia and was claimed in turn by the Achaemenids, Mauryans, Kushans, Ghaznavids, Timurids and Mughals, and in 1747 it became part of the Durrani Empire.
Babur made it his headquarters in 1504 and began his conquest of Hindustan from it in 1526, and in 1776 Timur Shah Durrani moved the capital of the Durrani Empire to Kabul from Kandahar.

After 1978 the city passed through revolution, Soviet occupation, a civil war that devastated about 80 percent of it by 1996, Taliban rule, the United States-led invasion of 2001 and the Taliban's return in 2021.
dyk: Babur loved Kabul and was initially buried in Agra, but following his wish he was later buried in Kabul.

sections.origins:
Kabul lies at an altitude of 1,791 metres in a narrow valley of the Hindu Kush, on the Kabul River, in the eastern half of Afghanistan. It is believed to be over 3,500 years old, though the origin of the city, who built it and when, is largely unknown. The Rigveda, composed between 2000 and 1500 BCE, and the Avesta refer to the Kabul River and to a settlement called Kubha. The meaning of the name is unknown. In Sanskrit the city was known as Kubha, and Greek authors of antiquity called it Kophen, Kophes or Koa; Ptolemy recorded it as Kabura, and the Greeks also called it Ortospana, "High Place". The Chinese monk Xuanzang recorded it as Gaofu, which Alexander Cunningham linked to one of the five tribes of the Yuezhi.

According to legend, a lake once lay in Kabul with an "Island of Happiness" in its middle, where a family of musicians lived and which a king made accessible by a bridge (pul) of straw (kah); the name Kabul is said to have formed from the two words. The Concise Oxford Dictionary of World Place Names calls a derivation from the Arabic root qbl, "meeting" or "receiving", unlikely. It is not known when the name was first applied to the city. It came into prominence after Genghis Khan destroyed Kapisa and other cities in the thirteenth century. The name was first applied to the river, and the area between the Hindu Kush and the Khyber Pass was also known as Kabulistan.
sections.growth:
Under the Achaemenid Empire Kabul became a centre of learning for Zoroastrianism, followed by Buddhism and Hinduism, and an inscription on the tomb of Darius the Great lists it among the 29 countries of the empire. Under the Mauryans trade flourished through the use of uniform weights and measures, public irrigation raised the harvest, and people worked as artisans, jewellers and carpenters. The Indo-Greek rulers patronised Buddhism, and the majority of the region's people followed it. In the late 14th century Kabul became a major trading centre in the kingdom of Timur.

Under the Mughals, who ruled it for about 200 years, Kabul became a prosperous urban centre with bazaars such as the Char Chatta, and a mint that struck gold and silver coins until the reign of Alamgir II. It served as a military base for Shah Jahan's campaigns in Balkh and Badakhshan, and the population was about 60,000. By the time of Ahmad Shah Durrani it had lost its metropolitan status, and an estimate puts its people at about 10,000 in 1700. Timur Shah and Zaman Shah built religious and public buildings and settled Sufis, jurists and literary families with land grants and stipends. The population was estimated at 65,000 in 1878, 120,000 in 1940 and about 500,000 in 1979. The built-up area reached 68 square kilometres by 1962, almost fourteen times that of 1925.
sections.rulers:
The Kabul Valley was part of the Median Empire and then, from 549 BCE, of the Achaemenid Empire. After Alexander and the Seleucids, the Seleucid Empire ceded it to the Maurya Empire in 305 BCE. The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom took it in the early 2nd century BCE and lost it to the Indo-Greeks around the middle of that century. The Indo-Scythians expelled the Indo-Greeks by the mid 1st century BCE and lost the city to the Kushan Empire in the first century CE. Around 230 the Sasanian Empire defeated the Kushans and installed vassals, the Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom. The Kidarites drove them out in 420, the Hephthalites replaced the Kidarites in the 460s, and the Tibetan Empire briefly held the city between 801 and 815.

The Islamic conquest reached modern Afghanistan in 642, when Kabul was independent under the Kabul Shahis. Ya'qub bin Laith as-Saffar took the city from the Hindu Shahis in 870, and it reverted to Shahi rule around 900. Sabuktigin took it permanently around 977. The Ghaznavids, Ghurids, Khwarazmshahs and Qarlughids followed, and the Mongols invaded in the 13th century. Babur captured Kabul in 1504 and the Mughals held it for the next 200 years. Nader Shah took it in 1738, and in 1747 Ahmad Shah Durrani asserted Pashtun rule. Timur Shah Durrani moved the capital from Kandahar to Kabul in 1776.

In 1826 Dost Mohammad Khan claimed the kingdom. The British reinstalled Shah Shuja Durrani in 1839,, and Akbar Khan took the throne from 1842 to 1845. Habibullah Khan, Amanullah Khan, Nader Khan and Zahir Shah, the last king of Afghanistan, ruled in the 20th century.
sections.life:
Kabul has historically been the most ethnically diverse city in the country, and Dari and Pashto are the main languages, with Dari long the lingua franca. Babur described eleven or twelve tongues spoken in the Kabul country, among them Arabic, Persian, Turkic, Mongolian, Hindi and Afghani, and tribes of Turks, Arabs, Sarts, Tajiks, Hazaras and Afghans. A National Geographic article of 2003 put the city's people at 45 percent Tajik, 25 percent Pashtun and 25 percent Hazara. About 90 percent follow Sunni Islam and 10 percent are Shias, mostly Hazaras in the Dashte Barchi area. Under the Kushans and the Indo-Greeks Buddhism was widely followed, and Istakhri in 921 described a castle with Muslims in it and a town with unbelievers from India. Records of religious correspondence show Jews in Kabul since the 8th century, and al-Idrisi wrote of a Jewish quarter in the 12th century. Most of the roughly 2,000 who remained in Afghanistan left after 1979, and none are believed to remain.

Houses were generally walled compounds built around courtyards, with narrow passageways. The Kabul River divides the central bazaars. In the 20th century the city modernised under Habibullah Khan, with electricity, telephone and a postal service, and the first modern high school, Habibia, was founded in 1903. Amani and Lycee Esteqlal were founded in the 1920s, and Kabul University opened in 1932. The city had leather and textile industries by 1916. In the second half of the century it became a stop on the hippie trail and was nicknamed the "Paris of Central Asia".
sections.crises:
The Mongol invasion of the 13th century caused major destruction in the region, and Genghis Khan destroyed Kapisa and other cities. Ibn Battuta, visiting in 1333, found Kabul formerly a vast town whose site was occupied by a village inhabited by Afghans. In the First Anglo-Afghan War a local uprising in 1841 killed the British resident, and in the retreat from Kabul to Jalalabad in 1842 Afghan tribesmen killed 4,500 regular British troops and 14,000 civilians. The British returned later that year and demolished the main bazaar in revenge. In the Second Anglo-Afghan War, which broke out in 1879, the Bala Hissar was partly destroyed by a fire and an explosion.

On 28 April 1978 President Daoud and most of his family were killed in the Saur Revolution. The Soviet Union invaded on 24 December 1979 and heavily occupied Kabul. A major uprising, the 3 Hut uprising, broke out in February 1980 and led to a night curfew that remained for seven years. The city's population rose from around 500,000 in 1978 to 1.5 million in 1988, largely from internal refugees. After the fall of Najibullah's government in April 1992 mujahideen factions entered the city, and shelling by Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's party escalated into the "Kabul Wars", in which at least 30,000 civilians were killed. About 80 percent of the city was destroyed by 1996.

The Taliban seized Kabul on 27 September 1996. In November 2001 the Northern Alliance captured the city after the Taliban left it, following an American invasion. The Taliban took it again on 15 August 2021.
sections.legacy:
Babur's tomb lies in the Gardens of Babur, the Bagh-e Babur, with its Persian couplet, "If there is a paradise on earth, it is this, and it is this, and it is this!" The gardens were rebuilt in 2005. Babur's writing on Kabul and the descriptions of Ibn Battuta, Istakhri and George Forster, who called 18th-century Kabul "the best and cleanest city in Asia", give a record of the city across centuries. Its buildings reflect its links with many empires. The Buddhist Chakari minaret was likely built in the Kushan era. The Mausoleum of Timur Shah Durrani is octagonal, and the Eidgah Mosque is a fine example of the Babur era. The Bagh-e Bala Palace was designed in a mixed Mughal and British Indian style, and the Darul Aman Palace, begun under Amanullah Khan, is the best known example of modern Western design.

The Kabul River still divides the central bazaars, though since the 21st century it has run dry most of the year. The old centre holds Bala Hisar, Deh Afghanan and Murad Khane. After 2001 many damaged landmarks were rebuilt or restored, including the Mahmoud Khan Bridge clock tower in 2013 and the Taj Beg Palace in 2021. Kabul is today the capital and largest city of Afghanistan, with an estimated population of about 5.3 million, and Dari and Pashto are spoken by most of its people.

summary: Kabul lies high in the Hindu Kush in eastern Afghanistan and is believed to be over 3,500 years old. Babur made it his headquarters in 1504, and Timur Shah Durrani made it the capital in 1776. It is now the capital and largest city of Afghanistan.
notes: START: the article says only 'believed to be over 3,500 years old' and that the Rigveda (2000-1500 BCE) refers to a settlement Kubha. I used c. 1500 BCE with circa true.
The article's Achaemenid/Median dates: Median Empire 'c. 678-549', Achaemenid 'c. 550-330'; I used 549 BCE (Cyrus) only.

Population: article gives 10,000 in 1700 and also says 10,000 after Ahmad Shah's rise; and 60,000 under the Mughals (undated within the period). 1979 'around 500,000' vs another source's 337,715 in 1976: I kept the 500,000 and left out the other figure. I left out the 2001-2014 figures.
The Chakari minaret is 'likely' Kushan, as hedged. The Mughal gardens and the Char Chatta bazaar 'have not survived/non-extant': omitted in text except as the article names Char Chatta.
Alexander: the article says only that the Kabul Valley came under his control; no date given. I left his conquest out of the dated lists and out of rulers' dates.

Rulers paragraph: I wrote 'After Alexander and the Seleucids' loosely; the article says Seleucus seized Alexander's empire. The article gives no dates for Nader Shah's hold beyond 1738 capture and 'nine years' later assassination (1747); I left the dates of his rule out except 1738.
Ibn Battuta 1333 quotation paraphrased as 'formerly a vast town ... occupied by a village inhabited by Afghans'; the article quotes 'a tribe of Persians called Afghans'. Check wording.

Taliban 1996: 'Kabul Wars' figure of at least 30,000 civilians and 80 percent devastation are the article's. The 1996-2001 Taliban measures (restrictions on women, punishments) are left out of the text for space; the editor may wish to add them as plain facts.
Soviet period: 1979 invasion, the 3 Hut uprising (curfew seven years) and 1978 coup given as bare dated facts. The Dubs kidnapping and the ISI/Operation Cyclone passage left out (claims contested).
Anglo-Afghan figures: 4,500 troops and 14,000 civilians killed in 1842 as the article states.

The Jewish community: the article says 'approximately 2,000' left after the 1979 invasion and that 'there are believed to be no Jews in Afghanistan' after November 2021; I wrote 'none are believed to remain'.

Recent events 2021-2025 (the Taliban return, 2025 drone strike) given as bare facts; the 2025 strike left out. Present mayor, ministers, airports, hotels, tourism, sports left out as the guide requires.
Population today 5,333,284 is given in the article without a year in the lead; I wrote 'about 5.3 million'. The article's estimates conflict on many dates (no census): hence the hedge 'estimated'.
Mongol destruction: the article's Bamiyan massacre passage is about Bamiyan, not Kabul; I left it out.
Abu Hanifa and other 'notable people' left out.
